In the beginner course you strung beads onto cord and wire. Advanced work is different: in bead weaving, every bead touches its neighbours, so **uneven beads show immediately**. In wire work and metal findings, the metal touches skin all day, so **the wrong metal causes green marks, tarnish or itchy ears**. Buying well is the first professional skill.

Seed beads and cylinder beads

Seed beads are sized with a number and a slash, such as **11/0** (say 'eleven aught'). The bigger the number, the smaller the bead: 15/0 is tiny, 11/0 is the everyday size for weaving, 8/0 and 6/0 are larger. Japanese brands such as **Miyuki** and **Toho** are known for very even size and large holes, which matters when your needle passes through the same bead three or four times. **Cylinder beads** (Miyuki Delica, Toho Treasure) are short tubes with straight sides. They sit flat and tight in peyote and brick stitch, which is why they are used for picture patterns and lettering.

Findings and metals: read the stamp
Findings are the metal parts: clasps, jump rings, ear wires, head pins, crimps and bails. The metal you choose decides how long a piece lasts and how kind it is to skin.
**Sterling silver** is stamped **.925**, meaning 92.5% silver mixed with other metal (usually copper) for strength. It tarnishes slowly but can be polished back.
**Gold-filled** is stamped like **14/20 GF**: a thick layer of 14 karat gold bonded to brass, making up one twentieth (5%) of the weight. It lasts for years with normal wear.
**Gold-plated** has a very thin layer that can rub off, especially on rings, clasps and ear wires. Price it and describe it honestly as plated.
**Copper and brass** are affordable and good for practice and rustic designs, but they darken over time and can leave green marks on some skin.
**Stainless steel, titanium and niobium** are popular choices for ear wires because they do not tarnish easily.
Nickel and sensitive ears

Nickel is one of the most common causes of skin allergy from jewellery, and it is often hidden in cheap base-metal findings. For earrings, use ear wires sold as nickel-free, or sterling silver, titanium or niobium. Never describe a piece as hypoallergenic unless the seller of the finding has stated it, and tell customers which metal you used.
How much to buy: count, do not guess

Bead counts per gram vary by brand, size and finish, so the most reliable method is to count a sample yourself. A small digital jewellery scale that reads to 0.01 g is one of the best investments you can make. Weigh 1 g of beads, pour them on a bead mat and count them in groups of ten.
Worked example: buying cylinder beads for a cuff
For example, Halima in Kaduna plans a peyote cuff that her pattern says needs about 3,000 cylinder beads in her main colour.
She weighs out 1 g of her chosen cylinder beads and counts them: 186 beads.
Grams needed: 3,000 ÷ 186 = 16.1 g.
She adds about 10% for spills, faulty beads and design changes: 16.1 × 1.1 = 17.7 g.
The seller packs this colour in 5 g tubes, so 17.7 ÷ 5 = 3.5, which means she must buy 4 tubes (20 g).
She buys all four tubes from the same batch at the same time, because colours can vary slightly between batches.
Halima buys 20 g in four tubes from one batch, enough for the cuff with a small safety margin, instead of running short halfway through.

**Flush cutters** have one flat side and one angled side. Always place the flat side toward the wire you are keeping, so the end on your piece is flat. Then check the end with your fingertip: if it catches, file it smooth with a fine needle file or a cup bur. Never cut steel memory wire or thick headpins with your jewellery cutters, because it dents the blades. Use heavy-duty memory wire cutters for that.
Protect your eyes when cutting wire

Cut wire ends can fly across the room. Wear safety glasses, point the cutter down toward the table, and cover the short end with a finger or your other hand as you cut. Keep small wire offcuts in a jar, not on the floor where children or bare feet can find them.
Needles, threads and the weaving kit
**Beading needles** size 10 or 12 for 11/0 beads; size 12 or 13 for 15/0 beads and bezels. They are long and thin, and they bend over time, so keep spares.

**Thread**: braided gel-spun thread such as Fireline (4 lb to 6 lb) is very strong and does not stretch, good for structure and bezels. Nylon threads such as Nymo, KO or One-G are softer and drape better in cuffs and ropes. Use a colour close to your beads.
**Thread conditioner** (beeswax or a synthetic conditioner) reduces tangles in nylon thread.
**Small sharp scissors** for nylon; Fireline dulls scissors quickly, so use an old pair or a thread cutter for it.
**Bead mat** (velvet or foam) so beads do not roll, plus small dishes for each colour.
Light, posture and breaks

Bead weaving with 11/0 and 15/0 beads strains eyes and shoulders. Work near a bright window during the day and use a white LED desk lamp at night, placed so your hand does not cast a shadow on your work (lamp on the left if you are right-handed). Sit with your elbows supported on the table and bring the work up toward you instead of bending your neck down. A simple rule many makers follow is to look up from close work at something across the room every 20 minutes, and stand and stretch every hour. If you need reading glasses or a magnifier, using one is a professional choice, not a weakness.

Proportion and weight

For example, Blessing in Benin City is making a coral-colour necklace for a customer attending a traditional wedding in a boat-neck outfit. The customer wants it to sit just below the collarbone.

The focal piece in the centre is a 30 mm carved pendant that replaces 3 repeats, so she needs 40 large beads and about 41 spacers.

Your cultural design identity

African bead traditions give you a deep design library: coral and red bead regalia associated with the Edo and other royal traditions, Krobo powder-glass beads from Ghana, waist beads, Ndebele beadwork from Southern Africa (which gives its name to the herringbone stitch you will learn), adire and ankara textile patterns, and bold geometric forms. Use these as inspiration with respect: learn what a symbol means before using it, avoid copying sacred or chieftaincy regalia for casual wear, and say honestly what your piece is, for example 'inspired by Ndebele colour blocking' rather than claiming it is traditional.
Wearability test before you sell
**Clasp**: can the wearer open and close it alone, with one hand, in under 30 seconds? Lobster clasps and toggles are easier than tiny spring rings.
**Movement**: lay a bracelet over your wrist and bend your hand. Stiff woven cuffs need a gentle curve so they do not dig in.
**Edges**: run a stocking over the piece. Snags mean a wire end or rough bead hole will catch on clothes.
**Hair and fabric**: wear it with a lace or knitted top for an hour. Pieces that pull threads or hair need smoother joins.
A signature is a repeated choice

Temper and work hardening

**Dead soft** wire bends very easily and is used for wrapping and weaving. **Half hard** wire springs back a little and holds its shape, which is why it is used for ear wires, clasps and frames. Every time you bend, hammer or pull wire, it becomes harder. This is called **work hardening**. Use it on purpose: shape a clasp in soft wire, then tap it a few times with a chasing hammer on a bench block to stiffen it. But if you bend the same spot back and forth too many times, wire becomes brittle and snaps. Plan each bend so you make it once.
Straighten without damage
To straighten kinked wire, pull it two or three times through nylon jaw pliers or a soft cloth held between finger and thumb. This also hardens it slightly, so straighten only what you need.
A simple framed stone pendant
Choose a flat-backed stone or cabochon, for example 25 × 18 mm, without holes.
Cut three pieces of 20 gauge wire long enough to go round the stone with extra for the bail (see the worked example). Straighten them and lay them side by side.
Bind the three wires together with 26 gauge wire at the bottom centre: 6 to 8 tight coils, pushed together so no gaps show.
Bend the bundle around the stone's outline, then bind again at each side with another 6 coils. Check the stone sits snugly inside.
At the top, bring the wires together. Bend the front and back wires over the face and the back of the stone to make prongs that stop it falling out.

Take the remaining wires up behind the top and roll them around round nose pliers or a pen to form a bail. Wrap the ends around the stem 2 or 3 times, trim with flush cutters and tuck the ends with chain nose pliers.

Almost every dangling earring, rosary-style chain and beaded link bracelet is built from loops. A loop that is off-centre or slightly open is the most common reason handmade jewellery looks cheap or falls apart. The goal is simple: **every loop the same size, centred and fully closed**.
Linked metal chain
Chains and linked bracelets are nothing more than many identical loops joined together.
Simple loop
Thread a bead on a headpin or a cut piece of wire.
Bend the wire 90 degrees right above the bead with your fingertip or chain nose pliers.
Trim the bent wire to about 1 cm with flush cutters (slightly less for 22 gauge, slightly more for larger loops).
Grip the very end in round nose pliers at the marked spot on the jaw, and roll the wire back toward the bead in one smooth movement.
Reposition and roll again until the loop closes, centred over the bead.

A simple loop can be opened sideways to attach a part, which makes it quick for earrings. But it can also open under strain. For anything that will be pulled, such as bracelets and necklaces, use a wrapped loop.
Wrapped loop
Leave about 4 to 5 cm of wire above the bead. Grip the wire with chain nose pliers about 3 mm above the bead and bend it 90 degrees. That 3 mm gap is where your wraps will sit.
Place round nose pliers at the bend and wrap the wire up and over the top jaw, then down around the bottom jaw to make a loop.
If you are joining to another part, slip it onto the open loop now.
Hold the loop flat in chain nose pliers and wrap the tail neatly around the stem 2 or 3 times, coils touching.
Trim the tail flush and press the end in so nothing sticks out.

Jump rings: twist, never pull

Hold the jump ring with two pairs of chain nose pliers, the opening at the top. Push one hand away from you and pull the other toward you, so the ends move sideways past each other. To close, reverse the movement and gently push past the closed point and back, so the ends click together with no gap. Pulling the ends apart sideways into a 'C' shape weakens the ring and it will never close neatly again.

Coils, spirals and woven wire are the techniques that make customers ask 'did you really make this by hand?'. They take more time and wire, so they belong on your higher-priced pieces. The skill is in **even tension and consistent spacing**, and in knowing how much wire you will use before you start.

Tight coils on a core

Hold a thicker core wire (18 or 20 gauge) and wrap thin wire (24 to 26 gauge) around it, each turn touching the last. Hold the start firmly with your thumb and keep the thin wire at a right angle to the core. Push the coils together with your thumbnail every few turns so no gaps show. A coiled section can be slid onto another wire as a decorative tube, used as a bracelet bar or bent into an ear-wire front.

She adds 10% for starting and finishing: 167 × 1.1 = about 184 cm, so she cuts 1.9 m.

Figure-of-eight weaving

Woven wire looks like fabric. Lay two 20 gauge frame wires side by side about 1 mm apart. Anchor a long piece of 26 or 28 gauge wire with three coils on the top frame wire. Then pass the thin wire over the top wire, down between the two, under and around the bottom wire, and back up between them: a figure of eight. Push each pass close to the last with your thumbnail. Count passes so both sides of a piece match. With three frame wires you can weave patterns such as 'one wrap on the top wire, then over two', which creates ridges.

Viking knit is a looped wire chain made by stitching fine wire (often 26 or 24 gauge) around a dowel in a series of petal-shaped loops, then pulling the finished tube through a wooden drawplate with holes of decreasing size to make it long, thin and even. It produces a supple, rich-looking chain but uses a lot of time and wire, so price it accordingly and use it as a hero piece rather than an everyday chain.

Peyote stitch (also called gourd stitch) makes a smooth, firm fabric where each bead sits half a bead higher than its neighbour, like a staggered wall turned on its side. Worked with cylinder beads, it gives the flat, tight surface used for patterned cuffs, bookmarks, pendants and bezels. Once you can read the 'up beads', peyote becomes calm and rhythmic.
A sewing needle and thread
Peyote is worked with a long beading needle, adding one bead at a time into the gaps of the row before.
Thread and needle set-up

Use a size 10 or 12 beading needle and about 1.5 m of thread: longer threads tangle and wear. For cylinder beads, 6 lb Fireline or a nylon thread such as KO or One-G works well. If using nylon, stretch it gently and pull it through conditioner. Pick up a **stop bead** (one spare bead), pass through it twice and slide it to about 20 cm from the end. It holds the first beads in place and you remove it later.
Working flat even-count peyote
Pick up an even number of beads, for example 10. These become rows 1 and 2 together, because peyote beads settle into two levels.
Row 3: pick up 1 bead, skip the last bead you strung, and pass through the next bead. Pick up 1, skip 1, pass through 1. Repeat to the end. You will add 5 beads.
Pull gently: the beads lift into a zigzag. The beads that stick up are **up beads**; the ones sitting lower are **down beads**.
Row 4 and every row after: pick up 1 bead and pass through the next up bead. Never pass through a down bead. Each row adds half the width, so 5 beads per row here.
Keep the tension firm but not tight enough to curl the fabric. Hold the work between finger and thumb close to where you are stitching.
Counting rows

Peyote rows run diagonally, which confuses everyone at first. Count the beads in one straight column along the edge and multiply by two: each column has a bead in every second row. A pattern chart shows rows the same way, so check your count against the chart every ten rows.

**Odd-count peyote** (an odd number of beads across) lets a pattern have a centre column, but at the end of every second row there is no up bead to step into, so you need an extra 'turnaround' path through the previous rows. Learn even-count first; most patterns for beginners at this level use it.
Adding and ending thread

When about 15 cm of thread remains, stop. Weave the old tail back through the beadwork in a zigzag path, following the existing thread path through 8 to 10 beads and changing direction at least twice, then trim close. Start the new thread about 10 rows back, weave through in a zigzag so it locks, and come out of the same bead the old thread left. Do not tie knots on the surface; the zigzag path and friction hold the thread. If you do use a knot, make a small half-hitch around the thread between beads and hide it inside a bead.
Worked example: planning a patterned cuff
For example, Ifeoma in Onitsha has a customer with a 15.5 cm wrist who wants a 4 cm wide peyote cuff in cylinder beads, closed with a sewn-on button and loop.
She weaves a test swatch 10 beads wide and 20 rows long, and measures it: 1.3 cm wide and 1.6 cm long.
Width per bead column: 1.3 ÷ 10 = 0.13 cm. For about 4 cm: 4 ÷ 0.13 = 30.8. Peyote needs an even count, so she chooses 30 columns (3.9 cm).
Length per row: 1.6 ÷ 20 = 0.08 cm. She wants 16 cm of beadwork (wrist 15.5 cm plus a little ease, with the button overlapping): 16 ÷ 0.08 = 200 rows.
Each row holds half the columns: 30 ÷ 2 = 15 beads per row. Total: 200 × 15 = 3,000 beads.
She uses her 1 g count from Module 1 to convert to grams and buys from one batch.
Ifeoma knows the cuff is 30 beads wide, 200 rows long and about 3,000 beads, so she can quote a price and a delivery date before starting.

Brick stitch looks like bricks in a wall: each bead sits between two beads of the row below. Unlike peyote, you do not stitch through beads of the previous row; you hook your needle under the **thread bridges** (the little loops of thread between beads). That makes brick stitch perfect for shaped pieces such as triangles, diamonds and the fringed earrings that are hugely popular for owambe parties and aso-ebi.
An orange diamond shape
Brick stitch shapes such as triangles and diamonds grow from a ladder row by adding or dropping beads at the edges.
Step 1: the ladder base
Pick up 2 beads and slide them to 20 cm from the tail. Pass through both again in the same direction so they sit side by side, holes parallel.
Pick up 1 bead. Pass through the previous bead and then back through the new bead, so it sits beside the others.
Repeat until the ladder has the number of beads you need, for example 9.
To straighten a wobbly ladder, pass back through the whole row once in a zigzag.
Step 2: brick stitch rows
Exit from the end bead of the ladder, pointing up. Pick up 2 beads.
Pass the needle under the **second** thread bridge from the edge (not the first), front to back, and back up through the second bead you picked up.
Go down through the first new bead and up through the second again to make the pair sit flat.
Pick up 1 bead, pass under the next thread bridge and back up through the bead. Repeat to the end of the row.
Because you started at the second bridge, each new row is one bead shorter. That is how a triangle forms naturally.

To **increase** instead, stitch two beads into the same thread bridge at the start or end of a row. To keep the width the same, add one extra bead at the end of the row stitched into the last bridge. Diamond earrings use increases for the bottom half and decreases for the top half.

Step 3: fringe

Fringe hangs from the ladder row. Exit downward from the first ladder bead, pick up the strand beads and a turn bead at the bottom, skip the turn bead and pass back up through all the strand beads and the ladder bead. Then step across to the next ladder bead through the top rows. Keep the thread snug but not tight, or the fringe will stiffen instead of swinging. A V-shaped fringe (longest in the middle) is the classic style.

Colour changes are easy because every bead is added one at a time: just pick up the colour the chart shows. Cylinder beads give the crispest picture in brick stitch, while round seed beads give a softer, more textured look.

Herringbone (Ndebele) stitch: flat bands and tubular ropes
Start flat herringbone from a ladder with an even number of beads
Work tubular herringbone with a correct step-up at the end of each round
Calculate rounds and beads for a rope necklace from a swatch

Herringbone stitch creates columns of beads that lean toward each other in pairs, making a 'V' or fishbone pattern. It is also called **Ndebele stitch**, after the Ndebele people of Southern Africa whose beadwork made it famous. Herringbone fabric drapes softly, and in its tubular form it makes beautiful beaded ropes that can replace a chain.
A string of beads
Tubular herringbone turns seed beads into a supple rope that can carry a pendant or stand alone.
Flat herringbone
Make a ladder with an even number of beads, for example 8. Exit up from the last bead.
Pick up 2 beads. Pass down through the next ladder bead, then up through the bead after it.
Pick up 2 beads, down through the next bead, up through the next. Continue across. Each stitch sits on top of two ladder beads.
At the end of the row, turn by looping around the thread at the edge and coming up through the last bead you added.
In every following row, pick up 2 beads, go down through the second bead of the stitch below, and up through the first bead of the next stitch.
The key rule: you always pick up **two beads**, and you always travel **down one column and up the next**. The pairs pull toward each other, which creates the herringbone lean.
Tubular herringbone
Make a ladder of 8 beads and join it into a ring by passing through the first and last beads again. This gives 4 stitches around.
Exit up from a ladder bead. Pick up 2 beads, go down the next bead, up the next. Repeat 4 times around.
**Step up**: at the end of each round, pass up through the bead below and also through the first bead added in this round. Without the step-up, the rope spirals out of control.
Hold the tube around a pencil or a short dowel for the first few rounds, so it keeps its shape.
Keep tension firm: herringbone opens gaps between columns if thread is loose.
Worked example: a herringbone rope necklace
For example, Grace in Jos wants a princess-length tubular herringbone rope, 45 cm finished, in 11/0 round seed beads with 4 stitches per round.

Her 1 g count is 110 beads, so 2,280 ÷ 110 = 20.7 g. With 10% spare: 22.8 g. She buys 25 g.
Grace plans 284 rounds and buys 25 g, and she marks every 50th round with a safety pin so she can track progress against her plan.

A **cabochon** (cab) is a stone, glass, shell or resin piece with a flat back and no hole. A beaded bezel is a cup of peyote stitch that rises around the cab and grips its edge, so you can set stones that cannot be strung. It combines what you learned about peyote with bead embroidery, and it is the heart of statement pendants, brooches and the centre of a beaded collar. Your own resin cabochons from Module 4 can be set this way too.
A gemstone cabochon
A beaded bezel lets you set a flat-backed stone or resin piece that has no hole.
Materials for one pendant
A cabochon, for example a 30 × 40 mm oval.
Stiff bead embroidery backing (such as Lacy's Stiff Stuff or a stiff interfacing) and a soft backing (such as Ultrasuede or thin leather) for the back.
11/0 and 15/0 round seed beads in one colour family, Fireline 4 lb or 6 lb, size 12 needle.
A strong craft glue for the cab, a bail or ring for hanging.
Using strong craft glues

Many strong jewellery glues contain solvents with a heavy smell. Read the label, use a small amount, keep windows open, avoid skin contact and keep the tube closed and away from children. Let the glue cure for the full time stated on the label before stitching.
Step by step
Glue the cab to the stiff backing, leaving at least 2 cm of backing all round. Let it cure as the label says (often overnight).

**Base round**: come up through the backing right next to the cab. Pick up 4 beads (11/0), lay them along the edge and go down through the backing. Come back up between bead 2 and 3 and pass through beads 3 and 4 again. Repeat all round. This is backstitch.
The base round must contain an **even** number of beads. When you close it, pass through the whole round once more to straighten it.
**Peyote up the wall**: exit a base-round bead, pick up 1 bead (11/0), skip a bead, pass through the next. Repeat around. This is tubular peyote, so step up at the end of each round.
After one or two rounds of 11/0, switch to 15/0 beads. Smaller beads make the round smaller, pulling the wall inward over the edge of the cab. Work rounds until the bezel grips firmly.
Trim the stiff backing close to the base round without cutting thread. Glue or stitch on the soft backing, and add a bail between the layers at the top.
Join the two backings around the edge with a brick-stitch-style edging: come up through both layers, pick up one bead and pass back through it, repeating all the way around.

For example, Amaka in Asaba is setting a 30 × 40 mm oval agate cab for a pendant order.

She strings 11/0 beads on a thread to 2 cm and counts 13 beads, so each bead takes about 20 ÷ 13 = 1.54 mm along the base round.
Beads in the base round: 110 ÷ 1.54 = 71.4. She rounds to the nearest even number: 72.
Each peyote round then holds half the base count: 72 ÷ 2 = 36 beads.
She plans 2 rounds of 11/0 (72 beads) and 2 rounds of 15/0 (72 beads), checking the grip after each 15/0 round.
Amaka knows her base round is 72 beads and each bezel round 36, so if a round ends with one bead short or extra she knows immediately that she missed a stitch.

For a brooch, stitch a pin back to the soft backing before you join the edge, positioned in the upper third so the brooch does not tip forward. Record the cab size, base count and number of rounds on your order card, because a customer who loves the piece will often ask for a matching smaller pair of earrings.

Jewellery resin starts as liquid and becomes a hard, clear plastic through a chemical reaction. Done well, it looks like glass and lasts for years. Done badly, it stays sticky, goes cloudy, or worse, gives the maker a skin allergy that stops her using resin for good. Accurate mixing and safety habits are the whole foundation of this module.

Polyester casting resin also exists, but it has a strong styrene smell and needs more protective equipment, so most home jewellery makers avoid it. This course uses jewellery-grade epoxy and UV resin.
Mixing epoxy exactly

Every brand states its own ratio, for example **1:1 by volume** or **2:1 by weight**. These are not interchangeable: Part A and Part B often weigh different amounts per millilitre, so a 1:1 volume ratio is not 1:1 by weight. Measure exactly the way the label says, using graduated plastic cups or syringes for volume, or a digital scale for weight. Then mix slowly for about three minutes (or as the label says), scraping the sides and bottom of the cup, because unmixed resin on the sides will never cure.
Worked example: measuring two different resins
For example, Ruth in Port Harcourt has two resin kits and needs 30 ml of mixed resin for a batch of pendants.
Kit A says 1:1 by volume. 30 ml ÷ 2 = 15 ml of Part A and 15 ml of Part B, measured in graduated cups.
Kit B says 2:1 by weight. She weighs instead: for about 30 g total, 30 ÷ 3 = 10, so 20 g of Part A and 10 g of Part B on her scale.
Last month she guessed and poured 17 ml of A and 13 ml of B from Kit A. Her ratio was 17 ÷ 13 = 1.3 to 1, not 1:1, and the pieces stayed sticky.
She labels each kit with the ratio in marker so she never mixes them up.
Ruth measures by the method on each label, and her pieces cure hard and clear instead of staying tacky.

Safety rules
Protect your skin, eyes and lungs

Uncured epoxy and UV resin irritate skin and eyes, and repeated contact can cause sensitisation: an allergy that may become permanent, so that even small exposures cause rashes. Always wear nitrile gloves and safety glasses, work with windows open and a fan blowing fumes away from you and out of the room, and read the safety information that comes with your brand. If resin touches your skin, wash it off straight away with soap and water. Do not use vinegar, acetone or alcohol on skin, because solvents can carry resin deeper into it. If resin gets in your eyes, rinse with clean running water for at least 15 minutes and seek medical help.
**Never work on the dining table or near food**, and never use kitchen cups or spoons for resin. Keep a separate labelled box of resin tools.
**Keep children and pets away** while you pour and while pieces cure.
**UV lamps**: do not look into the light and keep skin out of it while curing.
**Heat**: mixed epoxy warms up as it reacts. A large mass in one cup can get very hot, smoke or crack, so mix only what you can use within the working time.
**Storage**: close bottles tightly, keep them out of direct sun, and note the date opened.
Disposal

Never pour liquid resin down a sink or drain. Mix small leftovers of Part A and Part B in the correct ratio, let them cure solid in a disposable cup, then dispose of the hardened lump with household rubbish. Let gloves and stirring sticks harden before throwing them away.

Nigeria's heat matters too. In a hot room, epoxy thickens and starts to set faster, so work in the cooler part of the day, mix smaller batches and read the working time on your label as a maximum, not a target. High humidity can cause cloudiness or a slightly sticky surface with some resins, so avoid pouring on very humid days or in a steamy kitchen.

Silicone moulds let you make the same shape again and again: earring drops, cabochons for your beaded bezels, pendants and beads. **Open bezels** (shallow metal trays with a loop) are filled with resin like a tiny dish and become finished pendants. Both reward careful planning more than speed.

Mixing too much resin wastes money; too little leaves cavities half filled. Fill each mould cavity with water using a syringe and note how many millilitres it takes. Then dry the mould completely (water left in the mould makes resin cloudy). Add about 10 to 15% for what stays on the cup and stick.
Worked example: mixing for an earring mould
For example, Kemi in Akure has a six-cavity teardrop earring mould and a 1:1 by volume epoxy.
She fills one cavity with water from a syringe: 3 ml. Six cavities: 6 × 3 = 18 ml.

She dries the mould with a hair dryer on a cool setting and leaves it open for an hour before pouring.

Getting rid of bubbles
**Warm the bottles** (still closed) in a bowl of warm tap water for a few minutes before measuring. Warmer resin is thinner and releases bubbles more easily. Dry the bottles before opening.
**Stir slowly** in a folding motion instead of whipping.
**Let the cup stand** for a couple of minutes so bubbles rise.
**Pour in a thin stream** into one corner of the cavity and let it flow across.

**Pop surface bubbles** with a toothpick, or with a quick pass of a heat gun or small torch held moving and a few centimetres away. Never hold heat in one spot: it can scorch the resin, damage the mould or start a fire.
**Cover** the mould with a box to keep out dust, insects and hair while it cures.

Layers, curing and demoulding

For deep moulds or when adding inclusions, pour in layers: a thin first layer, wait until it is gel-like (soft but not liquid, often a few hours depending on the brand and temperature), place your inclusions, then pour the next layer. Each layer bonds to the one below. Leave the mould flat and still while curing. Demould only when the piece is hard and does not bend or dent with a fingernail, usually after the time on the label. Flex the silicone away from the piece rather than pulling the piece out. Some epoxies are hard enough to demould in a day but reach full hardness later, so wait before drilling or sanding.
Open bezels

Stick a strip of packing tape to the back of an open (backless) bezel, or use a closed bezel tray. Place the bezel on a level surface (check with a phone level app). Fill in two or three thin layers rather than one thick one, stopping just as the resin rises to a slight dome at the edges. If the resin overflows the rim, wipe it immediately with a gloved finger and a tissue.
Mould care

Clean moulds with sticky tape to lift dust, store them flat and away from sun, and keep them only for resin. Shiny moulds give shiny pieces; scratches in the mould appear on every piece you cast, so never scrape cured resin out with a knife.

Mica powder and glitter are fine particles. Open containers gently, keep your face away and avoid breathing the dust. Wear a dust mask if you work with powders often.
Sanding and polishing

Cast pieces often have a sharp lip or rough edge where the resin met the top of the mould. Sand **wet**, with wet-and-dry sandpaper and a little water, which keeps dust down and the paper from clogging. Work through the grits in order: 400 to remove the lip, then 800, 1200 or 1500, and finally 2000. Each grit removes the scratches of the one before, so do not skip. Rinse and dry between grits. Finish with a plastic polish or polishing compound on a soft cloth.
Sanding dust
Only sand fully cured resin, always wet, and wear a dust mask and glasses. Dry resin dust irritates lungs and skin.
Doming with UV resin

Sanding leaves the surface dull. To bring back a glass-like shine, apply a thin coat of UV resin with a toothpick, spreading it to the edge but not over it: surface tension makes a gentle dome. Pop any bubbles, cure under the lamp for the time on the label, and add a second thin coat if needed. Thin coats cure clear; a thick coat may stay soft underneath.

Doming also works on cabochons you will set in a beaded bezel from Module 3: a smooth, domed top reflects light and makes the colours of the inclusion look deeper. Work on a level surface, and keep a few cocktail sticks handy to guide resin into corners of square or heart shapes, where it tends to pull back. Wipe any drip from the back before curing, because cured drips are hard to remove without sanding.

Mark the hole position with a fine marker, at least 2 to 3 mm from the edge so it does not crack.
Hold the piece on a scrap of wood. Using a hand pin vice or small drill with a 1 mm bit, drill slowly and straight, adding a drop of water to keep it cool. Wear glasses and a mask.
Attach a jump ring by twisting it open, or glue a small screw eye in with a drop of resin.

Collections, photography, pricing and custom orders

Advanced techniques only pay when the pieces sell at prices that cover your skill and time. This module shows you how to plan a small collection, photograph shiny and tiny pieces well on a phone, price for retail, boutiques and consignment, and manage custom and bridal orders safely.

A collection is a small family of pieces that clearly belong together. It makes your work look planned and professional, helps customers buy more than one piece, and makes marketing easier because every post tells part of the same story. With the techniques in this course you can combine wire, bead weaving and resin into one recognisable family.
A person arranging a collection of items
A collection is planned as a family, not made one random piece at a time.
Four decisions that hold a collection together
**Theme or story**: a clear idea that guides choices, for example 'Ankara Garden' or 'Harmattan Gold'. Write it in one sentence.
**Palette**: two or three main colours, tested with real beads and resin side by side, used in every piece.
**Metal tone**: all gold-tone, all silver-tone or all copper. Mixed metals across one collection look accidental.
**A repeated element**: the same spiral, the same resin shape, the same herringbone stripe or clasp in every piece.
The price ladder

Plan pieces at different prices so different customers can buy into the same collection. The **hero piece** is the showstopper that gets attention in photos (a beaded bezel collar, a woven wire cuff). **Mid-range pieces** carry the look at a moderate price (a herringbone rope with resin pendant, a peyote cuff). **Entry pieces** are quick to make and easy gifts (resin studs, simple wire-wrapped drops). Many buyers come for the hero in your photos and leave with an entry piece; that is the ladder working.

Mid-range: herringbone rope with small ankara pendant (about 5 hours) and peyote cuff with matching stripe (about 7 hours). 2 pieces.

Entry: ankara resin studs (about 30 minutes per pair), wire-wrapped resin drops (about 1 hour per pair), and a linked bracelet with resin charms (about 2 hours). 3 pieces, plus a gift box set of studs and drops.

At about 3 hours of focused work a day around her other duties, the first full sample set takes about 26 ÷ 3 = 9 working days.

Make samples, then batches

Make one sample of every piece first and wear-test each one for comfort, weight and clasp ease. Fix the design, record materials and times, then make stock in batches: cast all the resin elements in one session, make all the wrapped loops in another. Batching also makes your colours more consistent because you mix resin once and use one batch of beads.
Checking cohesion before you launch

Lay all the samples together on a plain cloth and photograph them as a group. Then ask three questions. Does every piece share at least two of the four decisions (palette, metal, repeated element, theme)? Could a stranger tell which pieces belong together without being told? Is there a clear jump in effort and price between entry, mid-range and hero? If a piece fails, change its colours or finding, or leave it out and save it for a future collection. Removing one weak piece makes the rest look stronger.

Think about the customer too. A collection for office wear needs lighter earrings, shorter lengths and quieter colours than one for owambe and weddings. Write down who the collection is for in one line, for example "working women aged 30 to 50 who want something handmade for church and office", and test every piece against that line.

A first collection of five to ten designs is enough to look complete without overwhelming your time and money. You can add pieces in a second release once you see what sells.

Write three or four honest sentences that say what inspired the collection, the materials, and who it is for. For example: 'Ankara Garden brings the prints of a Saturday market into jewellery you can wear to the office and to owambe. Each piece holds real ankara fabric sealed in clear resin, with hand-woven glass seed beads and gold-tone findings.' Avoid claims you cannot support, such as 'real gold' for plated findings or 'traditional' for a modern design.
Record everything
Keep a collection sheet with every piece's name, materials, quantities, minutes, and photos of the sample. It becomes your pricing sheet, your reorder list and your proof of original design.

Advanced pieces take hours. If your price only covers beads and wire, you are working for free, and you will burn out. A good price covers **materials, your time, your running costs and a profit** for the business to grow, and still works when a shop takes a commission.
A person using a calculator
Price from your own costs and times, then check the price against the market.
The pricing build-up
**Materials**: everything in the piece, from your receipts: beads, wire, findings, resin, thread, packaging. Include a small share for wear on needles and sandpaper.
**Labour**: hours from your time log × an hourly rate you decide. Choose a rate you would accept from someone else for skilled work, and raise it as you get faster and better.

**Overhead**: a percentage for running costs such as data, transport to buy materials, electricity, tools wearing out, bank charges. Many small makers use 10 to 20%; work out your own from a month of expenses.
**Cost price** = materials + labour + overhead.
**Retail price** = cost price + profit markup (for example 30 to 50%), rounded to a clean figure.

Custom order process
**Brief**: collect occasion, date, outfit colours or a fabric sample, neckline, wrist and neck measurements, budget and delivery address on a simple order form.
**Design and quote**: send a sketch or a photo of similar past work, the materials, the price and the delivery date in one written message.

**Approval**: send a progress photo at a key stage (for example, after the bezel or the first rope section) so changes happen before the piece is finished.

In the beginner course you strung beads onto cord and wire. Advanced work is different.

Read the stamp
Findings and metals
Sterling silver: 92.5% silver
14/20 GF: 14 karat gold is 5% of the weight

Findings are the metal parts: clasps, jump rings, ear wires and head pins. Read the stamp.
Sterling silver is 92.5% silver, mixed with another metal, usually copper, for strength.
14/20 G F means gold-filled: 14 karat gold bonded to brass, making up one twentieth, or 5%, of the weight. It lasts for years.
Gold-plated has a very thin layer that can rub off. Price it and describe it honestly as plated.
Copper and brass are affordable and good for practice, but they darken and can leave green marks on some skin.

Nickel is one of the most common causes of skin allergy from jewellery. For earrings, use ear wires sold as nickel-free, or sterling silver, titanium or niobium, and tell the customer which metal you used.
Count, do not guess
How many grams of beads to buy
Buy the whole amount from one batch, at the same time.
Count the beads your pattern needs
Weigh 1 g and count it in groups of ten
Divide to find the grams you need
Round up to whole packs
Beads per gram change with brand and finish, so count a sample yourself on a digital scale that reads to 0.01 g.
Step one. Find how many beads your pattern needs.
Step two. Weigh 1 g of your beads, pour them on a bead mat and count them in groups of ten.
Step three. Divide the beads needed by your count to find the grams.
Step four. Add about 10% for spills, faulty beads and design changes.
Step five. Round up to the seller's pack size.
And buy it all from the same batch at the same time, because colours can vary slightly between batches.

Wire turns beads and stones into pendants, chains, connectors and clasps you make yourself.
A loop that is off-centre or slightly open is the most common reason handmade jewellery looks cheap or falls apart.
So the goal is simple. Every loop the same size, centred and fully closed.

Know your wire
Gauge and temper
Gauge (thickness)
Smaller number, thicker wire
18 gauge: about 1.0 mm
20 gauge: about 0.8 mm
26 gauge: thin, for coils
Temper (hardness)
Dead soft: wrapping and weaving
Half hard: ear wires, clasps
Bending makes wire harder
Too much bending: it snaps
Two things decide how wire behaves. First, gauge, which means thickness. The numbers run backwards. 18 gauge is about 1.0 mm. 20 gauge is about 0.8 mm. 26 gauge is thin, for coiling.
Second, temper, which means hardness. Dead soft wire is for wrapping and weaving. Half hard holds its shape, for ear wires and clasps.
Every bend makes wire harder. Bend the same spot too often and it snaps, so make each bend once.
Making a wrapped loop
Wrapped loops for anything pulled. Simple loops for earrings.
Leave 4 to 5 cm of wire above the bead
Grip 3 mm above the bead and bend 90 degrees
Wrap over round nose pliers to form the loop
Add the next part now, if joining
Wrap the tail 2 or 3 times, coils touching
Trim flush and press the end in
Step one. Leave about 4 to 5 cm of wire above the bead.
Step two. Grip the wire with chain nose pliers about 3 mm above the bead and bend it 90 degrees. That 3 mm gap is where your wraps will sit.
Step three. Place round nose pliers at the bend and wrap the wire over the top jaw and down around the bottom jaw to make a loop. Mark a spot on the jaw so every loop is the same size.
Step four. If you are joining to another part, slip it on now.
Step five. Hold the loop flat and wrap the tail around the stem 2 or 3 times, coils touching.
Step six. Trim the tail flush and press the end in so nothing sticks out.
Simple loops are quick and can be opened, so they suit earrings. A wrapped loop cannot pull open, so use it for bracelets and necklaces.
Jump rings
Twist, never pull
Do
Hold with two chain nose pliers
Twist the ends sideways
Close by reversing the twist
Do not
Pull the ends apart into a C
Leave a gap when closing
To open a jump ring, hold it with two chain nose pliers and twist the ends sideways, one hand away from you, one toward you. Reverse the twist to close it with no gap.
Never pull the ends apart into a C shape. It weakens the ring, and it will never close neatly again.

Bead weaving builds a flexible beaded fabric with a needle and thread, one bead at a time, without a loom.
Three stitches sit behind most beaded cuffs, earrings and ropes: peyote, brick and herringbone.
Then you combine them to set a cabochon, a stone with a flat back and no hole, for statement pendants.

Flat even-count peyote
Always pass through up beads. Never through a down bead.
Use about 1.5 m of thread and a stop bead
Pick up an even number of beads, e.g. 10
Row 3: pick up 1, skip 1, pass through 1
Up beads stick out; down beads sit lower
Each new row: pick up 1, through next up bead
Step one. Use a size 10 or 12 needle and about 1.5 m of thread, because longer threads tangle. Add a stop bead about 20 cm from the end.
Step two. Pick up an even number of beads, for example 10. These become rows 1 and 2 together.
Step three. For row 3, pick up 1 bead, skip the last bead you strung, and pass through the next. Repeat to the end. You add 5 beads.
Step four. Pull gently and the beads lift into a zigzag. The ones that stick up are up beads. The lower ones are down beads.
Step five. In every row after, pick up 1 bead and pass through the next up bead.
If an edge looks uneven, you probably passed through a down bead. Check every few rows with your fingertip. Unpicking two rows takes minutes. Unpicking twenty takes an evening.
Worked example
Planning a patterned peyote cuff
Here is how a professional plans. Ifeoma in Onitsha has a customer with a 15.5 cm wrist who wants a 4 cm wide peyote cuff.
She weaves a test swatch 10 beads wide and 20 rows long. It measures 1.3 cm wide and 1.6 cm long.
So each column is 0.13 cm. 4 divided by 0.13 is 30.8, and peyote needs an even count, so she chooses 30 columns.
Each row is 0.08 cm. For 16 cm of beadwork she needs 200 rows.
Each row holds half the columns, 15 beads. 200 times 15 is 3,000 beads. Now she can quote a price and a delivery date before she starts.

Three stitches
Brick, herringbone and bezel
Hook under thread bridges, not through beads. Start each row at the second bridge to shrink by one.
Always pick up 2 beads, go down one column and up the next. Step up at the end of every round.
Even-count base round, peyote up the wall, then smaller 15/0 beads to grip the cab.

Brick stitch looks like bricks in a wall. You hook your needle under the thread bridges, the little loops between beads. Start each row at the second bridge and every row is one bead shorter, so a triangle forms for fringed earrings.
Herringbone, also called Ndebele stitch, makes columns that lean in pairs. Always pick up two beads, go down one column and up the next.
In a tubular rope, step up at the end of every round. Without the step-up, the rope spirals out of control.
A beaded bezel holds a cabochon by its edge. Backstitch a base round with an even number of beads, work peyote up the wall, then switch to smaller 15/0 beads. They pull the wall in over the stone.
Safety first
Using strong craft glue
Let the thread carry the weight. Glue only keeps things in place.
Read the label and use a small amount
Keep windows open
Avoid skin contact
Close the tube, keep it from children
Let it cure for the full time stated
Bezels and rope ends often use strong craft glue, and many contain solvents with a heavy smell. Read the label, use a small amount and keep windows open.
Avoid skin contact, keep the tube closed, and keep it away from children.
Let the glue cure for the full time on the label before you stitch or wear the piece.
On rope ends, sew the thread through a loop inside the cap first, so the thread carries the weight and the glue only holds the cap.
Quality checks
Before you sell woven work
End threads with zigzag paths, no surface knots
Earring pairs made side by side, strands match
Rope columns straight, no gaps
Bezel passes the shake and press test
Check every woven piece. Hide thread ends with zigzag paths, not knots on the surface.
Make earring pairs side by side, because customers notice when one fringe is a bead longer.
Keep rope columns straight and tight. And shake and press every bezel. A loose cab is a returned order.
Key points
Remember
Peyote: through up beads, never down beads
Brick: start at the second bridge to decrease
Herringbone: 2 beads, and step up every round
Bezel: even base round, then smaller beads
A measured swatch gives exact bead counts
To remember. In peyote, pass through up beads only. In brick stitch, start at the second bridge to decrease.
In herringbone, pick up two beads and step up every round. In a bezel, use an even base round, then smaller beads. And plan from a measured swatch.

Resin jewellery: mix safely, cast clear, finish well
Resin jewellery: mix safely, cast clear, finish well.
This is the video for Module 4 of Advanced Beadwork and Jewellery Making.
Why safety comes first
Resin is a chemical product
Liquid turns into hard, clear plastic
Done well, it looks like glass for years
Done badly: sticky, cloudy pieces
Worst case: a skin allergy for life
Jewellery resin starts as a liquid and becomes a hard, clear plastic through a chemical reaction. You can preserve ankara fabric, flowers and prints inside it.
Done well, it looks like glass and lasts for years.
Done badly, it stays sticky or goes cloudy.
Or worse, the maker develops a skin allergy that stops her using resin for good. So accurate mixing and safety habits are the foundation.
Know it before you start
Protect skin, eyes and lungs
Nitrile gloves, safety glasses, windows open and a fan blowing fumes out of the room.
Wash it off straight away with soap and water. No vinegar, acetone or alcohol on skin.
Rinse with clean running water for at least 15 minutes and seek medical help.
Uncured resin irritates skin and eyes, and repeated contact can cause an allergy that may become permanent.
So every session, wear nitrile gloves and safety glasses, open the windows and use a fan to blow fumes out of the room.
If resin touches your skin, wash it off straight away with soap and water. Do not use vinegar, acetone or alcohol, because solvents can carry resin deeper into the skin.
If resin gets in your eyes, rinse with clean running water for at least 15 minutes and seek medical help.
Never work near food or with kitchen cups, and keep children and pets away.
A safe resin session
Never pour liquid resin down a sink or drain.
Read the ratio and the method on the label
Measure exactly: cups for volume, scale for weight
Mix slowly about three minutes, scrape sides
Pour, cover, and label the date
Step one. Gloves, glasses and open windows, every time.
Step two. Read your label. A ratio of 1:1 by volume is not the same as 2:1 by weight, because Part A and Part B often weigh different amounts.
Step three. Measure exactly the way the label says: graduated cups or syringes for volume, a digital scale for weight.
Step four. Mix slowly for about three minutes, scraping the sides and bottom. Unmixed resin on the sides will never cure.
Step five. Pour, cover the piece from dust, and label the date.
Let leftover resin cure solid in a disposable cup, then put the hard lump with household rubbish. In a hot room, epoxy sets faster, so mix smaller batches.
Worked example
Mixing for an earring mould
Here is a worked example. Kemi in Akure has a six-cavity teardrop earring mould and an epoxy mixed 1:1 by volume.
She fills one cavity with water from a syringe. It takes 3 ml.
Six cavities need 18 ml.
She adds 15% for what stays on the cup and stick, and rounds up to 22 ml so it divides easily.
So 11 ml of Part A and 11 ml of Part B. She dries the mould completely first, because water makes resin cloudy. She fills all six cavities with only a thin film left.
One cavity, measured with water: 3 ml
Six cavities: 6 × 3 = 18 ml
Add 15%, round up: 22 ml
1:1 by volume: 11 ml Part A, 11 ml Part B
Clear, not cloudy
Warm the closed bottles in warm water
Stir slowly, do not whip
Pour in a thin stream into one corner
Quick, moving heat passes only
Cover the mould while it cures
Warm the closed bottles in a bowl of warm tap water for a few minutes. Warmer resin is thinner and lets bubbles out.
Stir slowly in a folding motion. Whipping is the common cause of tiny bubbles.
Pour in a thin stream into one corner and let it flow across.
Pop surface bubbles with a toothpick, or a quick, moving pass of a heat gun. Never hold heat in one spot. It can scorch the resin or start a fire.
Cover the mould with a box to keep out dust, insects and hair.
Inclusions and a glossy finish
Prepare
Dry flowers completely
Seal ankara on both sides
Tiny amounts of colourant
Finish
Wet sand: 400 up to 2000
Thin UV resin dome for shine
Drill 2 to 3 mm from the edge
Inclusions must be completely dry. Seal ankara on both sides with a decoupage medium first, or it soaks up resin and turns dark and patchy. Use only a little colourant, so the resin still cures.
Sand only cured resin, always wet, with a dust mask and glasses. Work through the grits in order, from 400 up to 2000.
A thin coat of UV resin brings back a glass-like dome. Drill slowly, at least 2 to 3 mm from the edge, with glasses and a mask.
Key points
Remember
Measure exactly by the method on the label
Gloves, glasses and fresh air every time
Resin on skin: soap and water, never solvents
Cure leftovers solid; never down a drain
Seal inclusions; sand wet; dome with thin coats
To remember. Measure exactly by the label method. Gloves, glasses and fresh air every time. Wash resin off skin with soap and water.
Cure leftovers solid and never pour resin down a drain. And seal inclusions, sand wet, and dome with thin coats.

Price your jewellery so every sale pays you
Price your jewellery so every sale pays you.
This is the video for Module 5 of Advanced Beadwork and Jewellery Making: collections, photography, pricing and custom orders.
Why this matters
Skill only pays when the price is right
Advanced pieces take hours
Beads-only prices mean working for free
Shops take a commission from your price
Custom orders need a clear, safe process
Advanced pieces take hours of skilled work.
If your price only covers beads and wire, you are working for free, and you will burn out.
A good price must still work when a boutique keeps a commission.
And custom and bridal orders earn the most, but only with a clear process and safe payments.
Collections
Plan a collection with a price ladder
One theme, palette, metal tone, repeated element
Hero: one showstopper for photos
Mid-range: two or three pieces
Entry: quick pieces and easy gifts
Five to ten designs is plenty
A collection is a small family of pieces that clearly belong together. Give it one theme, two or three colours, one metal tone and one repeated element, like the same resin shape in every piece.
The hero piece is the showstopper, like a beaded bezel collar.
Mid-range pieces carry the look at a moderate price, like a peyote cuff.
Entry pieces, like resin studs, are quick to make. Many buyers come for the hero in your photos and leave with an entry piece.
A first collection of five to ten designs is enough.
Pricing build-up
What every price must cover
Materials from your receipts
Labour: hours × your hourly rate
Overhead: data, transport, electricity
Add a profit markup, e.g. 30 to 50%
First, materials, from your receipts: beads, wire, findings, resin, thread and packaging.
Second, labour. Hours from your time log, times an hourly rate you would accept from someone else for skilled work.
Third, overhead, a percentage for running costs like data, transport and electricity. Many small makers use 10 to 20%.
Add those three together and you have your cost price.
Then add a profit markup, for example 30 to 50%, and round to a clean figure. That is your retail price.
Worked example
A peyote cuff and a boutique offer
For example, Ifeoma prices her peyote cuff. A Lagos boutique offers consignment and keeps 30%.
Materials
Labour: 8 hours × 1,500
Overhead at 10%
Retail at 40% markup
Her 70% share on consignment
Her own figures. Naira prices are approximate.
Here is a worked example with Ifeoma's own figures. A boutique in Lagos offers to sell her cuff on consignment and keep 30% of the selling price.
Materials come to 5,500 naira. Labour is 8 hours at 1,500 naira, which is 12,000 naira.
Overhead at 10% is 1,750 naira, so her cost price is 19,250 naira.
With a 40% markup, she rounds the retail price to 27,000 naira.
But on consignment she would receive only 70%, which is 18,900 naira. That is 350 naira less than her cost. She would lose money.
To get her cost plus 20% profit after commission, the retail price must be 33,000 naira. She uses that one price everywhere, so she never undercuts the boutique.
Photos
Photograph shiny, tiny pieces
Soft window light, no flash
White card to bounce, black card for edges
Steady phone, timer, move closer
Five shots: hero, detail, scale, worn, back
Edit lightly; keep colours true
Shoot beside a window with no direct sun. Turn off the flash and room lights.
A white card bounces light into shadows. A black card just out of frame gives silver and resin a crisp edge.
Lean the phone on books and use the 3-second timer. Do not pinch to zoom. Move closer instead.
Take the same five shots of every piece: hero, detail, scale, worn and the back or clasp.
Never change bead colours or make silver look like gold. A customer who gets something different will ask for a refund.
Custom orders
Brief, quote, deposit, approve, deliver
Confirm every payment in your own bank or payment app.
Brief: date, colours, measurements, budget
Quote and delivery date in one message
Start only when the deposit shows
Send a progress photo for approval
Balance, delivery and a care card
For custom and bridal orders, collect a brief on a simple form: occasion, date, outfit colours, measurements and budget.
Send the design, price and delivery date in one written message.
Start only after the deposit is received. Many makers take 50% for custom work.
Send a progress photo at a key stage, so changes happen before the piece is finished. And add a buffer week before every deadline.
Collect the balance as agreed, and pack the piece with a care card.
Fake SMS alerts and edited transfer screenshots are common scams. Only release goods when you see the money in your own app. Never share your OTP, PIN or login details with anyone.
Key points
Remember
Hero, mid-range and entry pieces in one collection
Cost price = materials + labour + overhead
Check your consignment share covers cost and profit
One retail price across all channels
Never trust an SMS alert or screenshot
To remember. Build a collection with a price ladder. Price from materials, labour and overhead, then add profit.
Check your share after any commission. Keep one retail price everywhere. And confirm every payment in your own bank app.
